title: Meßkirch to Todtnauberg: the Sexton's Son, the Rectorate, and the Hut
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Meßkirch, the sexton's house beside St Martin's
stops.date_confidence: attested. Coordinates approximate the Mesmerhaus and Stadtpfarrkirche St. Martin cluster in the old town of Meßkirch; the pin is derived from Schloss Meßkirch, adjacent to both, and is not surveyed to the building.
stops.campa: Friedrich Heidegger keeps the barrels of Meßkirch in repair and the bells of St Martin's on time. In the Mesmerhaus beside the parish church his first son is born on the twenty-sixth of September, into a Catholic household where the liturgical year is not a belief but a timetable. Sixty years on he will still be writing about this ground, the church and the field path out of town, as though thinking itself grew here. For now Johanna Heidegger raises him in the house attached to the bell tower, within earshot of the hours his father keeps.
suggested_refs: The Mesmerhaus and the Stadtpfarrkirche St. Martin at Meßkirch, his father's church and his birthplace

stops.name: Konstanz, the Konradihaus and the scholarship
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year 1903 and the residence 1903-1906; month and day are a convention for the start of a school year, not a documented date.
stops.campa: At fourteen he leaves home on a church scholarship and boards at the Konradihaus in Konstanz, the seminary residence that keeps boys the diocese intends for the priesthood, while attending the Heinrich-Suso-Gymnasium. Greek and Latin are paid for by an institution expecting a return. His father's wages cannot reach this far; the Church can, and does, and the arrangement is understood by everyone including the boy. A small-town child is quartered in a cathedral city and set to learn the languages in which Europe has argued about being. He boards there three years.
suggested_refs: The Konradihaus, Uhlandstraße 15, Konstanz, seminary boarding house of the archdiocese

stops.name: Freiburg im Breisgau, the Berthold-Gymnasium
stops.date_confidence: the transfer is attested to 1906, contradicting one chronology that dates it to 1909; 1909 is the year he finished school and matriculated. The coordinate is the Gymnasium's present Hirzbergstraße site; its pre-1965 location was not verified in this pass, so the pin is unresolved rather than exact.
stops.campa: After three years at Konstanz he transfers to the Berthold-Gymnasium in Freiburg im Breisgau and lodges again in a church seminary, still on the Church's account, still pointed at ordination. Freiburg will hold most of the next seventy years of his life: his degrees, his chair, his rectorate, his disgrace, his death. For now he is a schoolboy in a borrowed bed, finishing a classical education somebody else is paying for. He leaves the Gymnasium in 1909 and enrolls at the university in the same city.
suggested_refs: The archiepiscopal seminary at Freiburg, his lodging from 1906

stops.name: Tisis near Feldkirch, two weeks in the novitiate
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1909; the day of entry and the day of discharge are not given in the reachable sources. Coordinates are the Tisis district of Feldkirch.
stops.campa: In September he presents himself at the Jesuit novitiate at Tisis, outside Feldkirch across the Austrian border, to begin the training that would make him a priest of the Society of Jesus. Within about two weeks he is discharged. The reason given is a heart condition, the same classification that will keep him out of the infantry in the war to come. Neither the day of entry nor the day of discharge survives in anything reachable. He crosses back over the border and enrolls in Catholic theology at Freiburg.
suggested_refs: The Jesuit house at Tisis, Feldkirch, and the Stella Matutina complex

stops.name: Freiburg, the theology course abandoned
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1911; month and day default. Coordinates are Kollegiengebäude I of the University of Freiburg, used throughout this file for the university.
stops.campa: Two years into the theology faculty a second bout of illness ends the clerical course for good. He transfers to philosophy, mathematics and the natural sciences, and the scholarship that has carried him since he was fourteen stops carrying him. What breaks here is a career, not yet a faith. The separation from confessional Catholicism takes another decade at least, and he will be buried by a priest in his father's parish. When he stopped being a Catholic, or whether he ever finished stopping, is not a question the record settles.
suggested_refs: The theology faculty of the University of Freiburg, 1909-1911

segments.name: Freiburg: The Apprenticeship and the Lost Chair

stops.name: Freiburg, the dissertation against psychologism
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1913; month and day default.
stops.campa: He takes his doctorate under Arthur Schneider with Die Lehre vom Urteil im Psychologismus, arguing that the validity of a judgment is not a fact about anybody's mental events. The target is the reduction of logic to psychology; the tools are neo-Kantian. Behind them stands Edmund Husserl, who had made the same attack a decade earlier and whom Heidegger has read closely for years without ever meeting him. Nobody in Meßkirch has heard of the discipline he is now in. He is twenty-three years old and two years out of the seminary.
suggested_refs: Die Lehre vom Urteil im Psychologismus (Freiburg dissertation, 1913)

stops.name: Freiburg, habilitation on a book Duns Scotus did not write
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1915; month and day default.
stops.campa: Under Heinrich Rickert he habilitates with Die Kategorien- und Bedeutungslehre des Duns Scotus, a study of a medieval treatise on the modes of signifying then universally credited to Duns Scotus. Later scholarship reassigns the text to Thomas of Erfurt. He has therefore written his qualifying thesis on a philosopher who did not write the book, which was the ordinary condition of medieval philology in 1915 and not a mistake of his own. The venia legendi follows. He may teach.
suggested_refs: Die Kategorien- und Bedeutungslehre des Duns Scotus (habilitation, 1915), the text now attributed to Thomas of Erfurt

stops.name: Freiburg, the Catholic chair goes to another man
stops.date_confidence: attested to 23 June 1916.
stops.campa: On the twenty-third of June the Freiburg chair for Catholic philosophy goes elsewhere. He had been groomed for exactly this post, the Church's candidate for the Church's professorship, and its loss cuts the last institutional cord to the confession that educated him. Twenty-six years old, doctorate and habilitation both in hand, he has just been declared surplus by the institution that arranged his entire training. He stays on in Freiburg without a chair and without a patron, lecturing as a Privatdozent.
suggested_refs: The Freiburg chair of Catholic philosophy, contested 1916

stops.name: Freiburg Münster, the marriage to Elfride Petri
stops.date_confidence: attested to 21 March 1917 in the Freiburg Münster, officiated by Engelbert Krebs; the Protestant ceremony of 25 March 1917 took place at Wiesbaden and is folded into this stop rather than given a pin of its own.
stops.campa: On the twenty-first of March, in the Freiburg Münster, Engelbert Krebs marries him to Elfride Petri, a Lutheran from a Prussian military family. Four days later the couple repeat the ceremony at Wiesbaden before a Protestant minister. The double wedding is the shape of the marriage: two confessions held in one household, neither giving way. Elfride will manage the money and commission the hut at Todtnauberg five years from now, and she will hold the household together through a rectorate, a second war and a denazification. The marriage lasts until his death in 1976.
suggested_refs: The Freiburg Münster, site of the Catholic ceremony of 21 March 1917

stops.name: The western front, the weather station
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The posting to a meteorological unit in 1918 is reported but no named unit or station could be corroborated; the coordinate is a rough Ardennes and Meuse-sector placeholder and marks no verified place.
stops.campa: Called up in 1915 to postal and weather-service duties, he spends the last year of the war attached to a meteorological unit behind the western front. His cardiac classification keeps him out of the infantry, and nobody shoots at him. No named unit and no precise station survive in the reachable record, and the coordinate here marks no verified place. What the work consists of is measurement: pressure, wind, cloud, readings taken so that gas and artillery can be aimed with the weather rather than against it.
suggested_refs: German army meteorological service on the western front, 1918

stops.name: Freiburg, assistant to Husserl
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1919; month and day default.
stops.campa: Husserl takes him on as assistant, and a decade of reading becomes an apprenticeship conducted face to face. The older man treats him as the heir of the phenomenological movement. Heidegger, lecturing on Aristotle, on Paul's letters, on the factical life of the human being, is already dismantling the master's transcendental ego from inside the master's own method. He has published nothing of consequence and is the most talked-about teacher in the country. Students come across Germany for the courses, and the courses circulate afterwards as typescripts, passed from hand to hand.
stops.quote: If the following investigation has taken any steps forward in disclosing the 'things themselves,' the author must first of all thank E. Husserl, who, by providing his own incisive personal guidance and by freely turning over his unpublished investigations, familiarized the author with the most diverse areas of phenomenological research during his student years in Freiburg.
stops.quote_source: Martin Heidegger, Being and Time, trans. Macquarrie and Robinson (1962), p. 489 note, quoted by Heidegger within the Der Spiegel interview of 1966
suggested_refs: Husserl's philosophy seminar at Freiburg, 1919-1923
sources: Der Spiegel interview (1966), trans. William J. Richardson, ditext.com/heidegger/interview.html

segments.name: The Hut and Marburg: Sein und Zeit

stops.name: Freiburg, the Natorp Report on Aristotle
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1922; month and day default.
stops.campa: To support his candidacy for a chair he writes out at speed a prospectus of his Aristotle interpretation for Paul Natorp at Marburg, the Phänomenologische Interpretationen zu Aristoteles. It is not a book about Aristotle. It is a plan for reading the Greek texts as though they were still undecided, still capable of saying something the tradition has spent two thousand years covering over. The typescript circulates, does its work, and secures Marburg. The book it announces is never published under that title.
suggested_refs: Phänomenologische Interpretationen zu Aristoteles, the Natorp Report of 1922

stops.name: Todtnauberg, the hut on the slope
stops.date_confidence: the completion date of 9 August 1922 and the carpenter Pius Schweitzer are attested. The coordinate is approximate and disputed within the sources consulted, which give two values roughly 1.4 km south of Todtnauberg village centre; no surveyed pin for the hut exists in them.
stops.campa: Elfride secures the ground and commissions the carpenter Pius Schweitzer; on the ninth of August the hut above Todtnauberg is finished. Three rooms, no running water, a well fed through a wooden pipe. He will write here for fifty-four years, in ski clothes through the winter, cut off by snow for weeks at a stretch. The hut becomes an argument in itself: the philosopher who thinks where the woodcutters live, photographed in his own doorway, and the photographs are also work. Below the window the Black Forest falls away toward the valley.
suggested_refs: The Hütte at Todtnauberg, completed 9 August 1922 by Pius Schweitzer

stops.name: Marburg, the associate chair
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1923; the month is the conventional start of the winter semester, not a documented date.
stops.campa: He takes the associate professorship at Marburg, his first chair, and finds there the New Testament scholar Rudolf Bultmann, who will spend the next five years learning to read scripture through categories Heidegger is still inventing. The lecture courses of these years are the workshop: time, death, everydayness, the dismantling of inherited ontology, delivered to rooms that fill early. Students take dictation. What they are writing down, in pieces and out of order, is the book that does not yet exist.
suggested_refs: The Marburg lecture courses, 1923-1928, later Gesamtausgabe volumes 17-26

stops.name: Marburg, the student Hannah Arendt
stops.date_confidence: the sources conflict: one dates the beginning to 1925, another to 1924, and the disagreement is not resolved here. Month and day default.
stops.campa: A student of eighteen, Hannah Arendt, comes to Marburg to hear the lectures. He is thirty-five, married, the father of two boys, and her teacher. The affair is conducted in secrecy and by arrangement, with signals for when she may come to his room; the letters survive, most of them his. Sources put the beginning at 1924 and at 1925 and do not agree. She leaves Marburg for Heidelberg and Karl Jaspers. Whether the word for what happened is love, or the abuse of a chair, has been argued for a century by readers of the same letters.
suggested_refs: The Arendt-Heidegger correspondence; Elzbieta Ettinger and Antonia Grunenberg on the relationship

stops.name: Marburg, Sein und Zeit
stops.date_confidence: 1927 is certain, the month is not: one source gives January 1927, another February 1927, and the Jahrbuch volume itself carries only the year. The date here is defaulted rather than adjudicated. The place marks where he was based while finishing the manuscript; the journal was printed by Niemeyer at Halle.
stops.campa: Sein und Zeit appears in Husserl's Jahrbuch and as a separate volume, dedicated to Husserl. It prints two divisions of a projected two-part work; the rest is announced and never delivered. Dasein, being-toward-death, the they, care, the ontological difference: the vocabulary arrives whole, in a German that grinds and hyphenates until the reader must slow to the speed of the sentence. He is thirty-seven and it is his first book. Marburg promotes him to full professor on the strength of it.
stops.quote: To counter widely circulated allegations, let it be stated here explicitly that the dedication of Being and Time ... remained in Being and Time until its fourth edition of 1935.
stops.quote_source: Heidegger, Unterwegs zur Sprache, trans. Peter D. Hertz (1971), p. 199, quoted by Heidegger within the Der Spiegel interview of 1966. The dedication was removed in the printing of 1941 and restored in 1953.
suggested_refs: Sein und Zeit, Jahrbuch für Philosophie und phänomenologische Forschung VIII (1927); the removal of the Husserl dedication in 1941 and its restoration in 1953

segments.name: Husserl's Chair, the Nothing, and Davos

stops.name: Freiburg, succeeding Husserl in the chair
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1928; month and day default.
stops.campa: Husserl retires and Heidegger is called back to Freiburg to take the chair, the succession the older man wanted and worked for. The pupil holds the teacher's post at thirty-eight, nine years after arriving as his assistant. Five years from now the state will strip Husserl of his university privileges. What Freiburg has appointed is in any case not a continuation: Sein und Zeit had already replaced the transcendental ego with something mortal, historical and thrown, and the dedication page said friendship while the book said otherwise.
suggested_refs: The Freiburg chair of philosophy, held by Husserl 1916-1928 and by Heidegger from 1928

stops.name: Freiburg, the inaugural lecture on the nothing
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1929; the month and day are not fixed in the sources used here, so the stop is defaulted to the start of the year and stands before the Davos disputation in this segment for that reason alone.
stops.campa: The inaugural lecture in the Aula asks what metaphysics is and answers by way of the nothing. Science concerns itself with beings and nothing besides, he says, and that nothing besides is where the question begins. Anxiety is the mood in which beings as a whole slip away and the nothing announces itself. Rudolf Carnap will take the lecture apart sentence by sentence as the exemplary metaphysical pseudo-statement, a nonsense produced by treating the word nothing as a noun. Each man believes the other has missed the point entirely.
suggested_refs: Was ist Metaphysik? (Freiburg inaugural lecture, 1929); Carnap's 'Überwindung der Metaphysik durch logische Analyse der Sprache' (1932)

stops.name: Davos, the disputation with Cassirer
stops.date_confidence: attested. The Davos Hochschulkurse ran 17 March to 6 April 1929 and the disputation itself is dated 26 March 1929, in the Konversationssaal of the Grand Hotel Belvédère. The coordinate is the canonical Davos pin used elsewhere in this corpus, a town-level value; the Belvédère itself geocodes about 800 m away at 46.8005, 9.8261.
stops.campa: In the Konversationssaal of the Grand Hotel Belvédère, before students gathered from across Europe, he disputes with Ernst Cassirer over what Kant was doing. Cassirer reads the Critique as the ground of a culture of symbolic forms, the Enlightenment still open and still working. Heidegger reads it as a book about human finitude that lost its nerve, and says so to the man's face. The students carry away the sense of a generation changing sides in a hotel ballroom. Kant und das Problem der Metaphysik is published later the same year.
suggested_refs: Kant und das Problem der Metaphysik (1929); the transcript of the Davoser Disputation, Gesamtausgabe 3

segments.name: The Rectorate and What Followed It

stops.name: Freiburg, the first of the black notebooks
stops.date_confidence: the notebooks are attested as beginning in 1931 and running into the 1970s; no month or day of first entry is given, and the date here orders the segment rather than marking an event.
stops.campa: He begins keeping notebooks in black oilcloth covers, private, numbered, written alongside the published work and withheld from it. They run from 1931 into the 1970s and he leaves instructions that they close the collected edition rather than open it. When Peter Trawny brings out the first of them in 2014 as volumes 94 to 102, the pages are found to contain antisemitic passages tying world Jewry to the machination and calculation his philosophy of technology attacks, and the argument about his politics stops being an argument about one year in office.
suggested_refs: Schwarze Hefte, Gesamtausgabe 94-102, ed. Peter Trawny, from 2014

stops.name: Freiburg, elected rector
stops.date_confidence: attested to 21 April 1933.
stops.campa: On the twenty-first of April, the Social Democrat Wilhelm von Möllendorff having resigned under political pressure, the Freiburg faculty elects Heidegger rector. He takes office while the new regime is purging the German universities. Thirty-three years later he will tell Der Spiegel that he had no administrative experience, that colleagues pressed the office on him, that he took it to keep worse men out. He will join the Party ten days from now. He holds the rectorate until April of the following year.
stops.quote: I protested that I had absolutely no administrative experience.
stops.quote_source: Heidegger, Der Spiegel interview 'Nur noch ein Gott kann uns retten' (1966), trans. William J. Richardson, describing von Möllendorff's demand that he take the rectorate
suggested_refs: The Freiburg rectorate, 21 April 1933 to April 1934
sources: Der Spiegel interview (1966), trans. Richardson, ditext.com/heidegger/interview.html

stops.name: Freiburg, party member 3,125,894
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1 May 1933; the membership number 3,125,894 is given in the dossier's verified sequence.
stops.campa: On the first of May, the day the regime has made a national holiday of labour, the rector of Freiburg joins the National Socialist German Workers' Party. His membership number is 3,125,894. The rectorate lasts one year; the membership lasts twelve, and everything he says afterward about 1933 has to be said across that arithmetic. He pays his dues until the Party ceases to exist in 1945. There is no record of a resignation: no letter, no lapse, nothing in the files.
stops.quote: At that time I saw no other alternative.
stops.quote_source: Heidegger, Der Spiegel interview (1966), trans. Richardson, on accepting the rectorate and praising the new era in 1933
suggested_refs: NSDAP membership records for Freiburg, 1933-1945

stops.name: Freiburg, the rectoral address in the Aula
stops.date_confidence: attested to 27 May 1933.
stops.campa: In the Aula on the twenty-seventh of May he delivers Die Selbstbehauptung der deutschen Universität. The university asserts itself, he argues, by binding knowledge to labour service and to military service and to the historical mission of the German people; the much celebrated academic freedom is repudiated as merely negative. He is forty-three years old and has held the rectorate five weeks. The address is printed, distributed, and read across Germany as a philosopher's ratification of the new state.
stops.quote: The much celebrated 'academic freedom' is repudiated by the German university; for this freedom was not genuine, insofar as it was only a negative one.
stops.quote_source: Heidegger, Die Selbstbehauptung der deutschen Universität (rectoral address, 27 May 1933), quoted verbatim by the Der Spiegel interviewers in 1966 and confirmed by Heidegger, trans. Richardson
suggested_refs: Die Selbstbehauptung der deutschen Universität (1933); Jacques Derrida, De l'esprit: Heidegger et la question (1987), which tracks the word Geist through Heidegger's writing to this address

stops.name: Leipzig, the professors declare for Hitler
stops.date_confidence: the date of 11 November 1933 and the city are attested; the hall is not. One source names the University of Leipzig as the venue, which the verification pass rejects, so the pin is city-level.
stops.campa: He travels to Leipzig for the rally of German professors declaring for Hitler ahead of the plebiscite on withdrawal from the League of Nations, and speaks within it. Hundreds of academics sign; the press carries it as the intellect of the nation ratifying the state. He is at the height of his public political usefulness, and it has five months left to run. The hall is not identified in anything reachable, so the pin here marks the city only. In the same season a Freiburg student newspaper prints a message over his name telling students where their law now resides.
stops.quote: Let not doctrines and ideas be the rules of your Being. The Fuhrer, himself and he alone, is today and for the future German actuality and its law.
stops.quote_source: Heidegger, statement in a Freiburg student newspaper, autumn 1933, quoted verbatim by the Der Spiegel interviewers in 1966; Heidegger disowned the sentiment but did not dispute the wording
suggested_refs: The Leipzig declaration of German professors, 11 November 1933

stops.name: Freiburg, the resignation of the rectorate
stops.date_confidence: attested to April 1934; the sources give 23 and 27 April for different steps of the resignation and the discrepancy is not resolved here.
stops.campa: He resigns the rectorate after a year, in a quarrel with Party officials over who may be dean of which faculty. He does not resign from the Party, and Karl Löwith will testify that the badge stays on the lapel at least two more years. Afterwards, and for the rest of his life, he presents the year as a protective manoeuvre, an attempt to hold the university out of worse hands; archival scholarship has found that account incomplete rather than false. He goes back to lecturing.
stops.quote: The sentences you quote I would no longer write today. Such things as that I stopped saying by 1934.
stops.quote_source: Heidegger, Der Spiegel interview (1966), trans. Richardson, responding to his 1933 statement on the Führer as German law
suggested_refs: Heidegger's 1945 account 'Das Rektorat 1933/34: Tatsachen und Gedanken'

stops.name: Freiburg, the inner truth and greatness
stops.date_confidence: the 1935 lecture course is attested; month and day default. Whether the parenthetical gloss stood in the 1935 manuscript or was added for the 1953 printing is disputed: Heidegger claimed the former in 1966, the disputed manuscript page is missing from the Marbach archive, and the standard scholarly view is against him.
stops.campa: In the summer lecture course later published as Einführung in die Metaphysik he speaks of the inner truth and greatness of the National Socialist movement. When the course is printed in 1953 the phrase carries a parenthesis glossing that greatness as the encounter of planetary technicity with modern man. Heidegger tells Der Spiegel the parenthesis stood in his 1935 manuscript. The page in question is not in the Marbach archive. Scholars generally hold that it was not there, and nobody can produce the sheet either way.
stops.quote: What today ... is bandied about as the philosophy of National Socialism but has absolutely nothing to do with the inner truth and greatness of this movement (namely, with the encounter between technicity on the planetary level and modern man) casts its net in these troubled waters of 'values' and 'totalities'.
stops.quote_source: Heidegger, Einführung in die Metaphysik (1935 lecture course, published 1953), read out by the Der Spiegel interviewers in 1966, trans. Richardson after Manheim. The ellipsis marks the interviewer's interjection.
suggested_refs: Einführung in die Metaphysik (1953); the missing manuscript page in the Deutsches Literaturarchiv Marbach

stops.name: Rome, the badge and Karl Löwith
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1936; month, day and venue are not recorded, and the coordinate marks central Rome only.
stops.campa: In Rome he meets Karl Löwith, once his student at Marburg, now a Jewish émigré out of Germany. He is wearing a swastika pin. Löwith writes the conversation down in a memoir of 1940: that Heidegger still held his political commitment to follow from his philosophy, and still expressed confidence in Hitler. The meeting falls two years after the resignation he would later describe as a break. It is not a court finding and it is not a document Heidegger signed; it is a contemporary witness with reason to remember exactly, writing it down four years afterwards and out of the country.
suggested_refs: Karl Löwith, Mein Leben in Deutschland vor und nach 1933 (written 1940)

stops.name: The Rhine plain west of Freiburg, the Volkssturm ditch
stops.date_confidence: attested to autumn 1944; the month is a convention and the coordinate is a rough placeholder for the Rhine-plain fortification works, not a verified site.
stops.campa: In the autumn the professor of philosophy, fifty-five years old, is drafted into Volkssturm labour digging anti-tank fortifications on the Rhine plain west of Freiburg. The university had earlier shielded its senior faculty from full deployment; that shelter is gone. Within months the French army is across the Rhine and in the city, and the men who classified him as dispensable will be replaced by men who classify him again. Which stretch of ditch he dug is recorded nowhere reachable, and the pin here is a placeholder for the works rather than a site.
suggested_refs: The Westwall labour drafts of autumn 1944 in Baden

stops.name: Freiburg, the denazification committee
stops.date_confidence: the Freiburg committee's dismissal of him from the university is dated September 1945; the day is not given. The formal French-zone teaching ban is a separate and later act, dated 5 October 1946, and one source wrongly collapses the two into 1945.
stops.campa: The Freiburg committee opens its examination and dismisses him from the university in September. Karl Jaspers, his friend of twenty years, is asked for an assessment and gives one that separates the stature of the thinking from the reliability of the man, recommending exclusion from teaching for a period. Heidegger offers the rectorate as obstruction: appointments blocked, a book-burning forbidden. The French Military Government's formal teaching ban is dated the fifth of October 1946, a year later.
stops.quote: I forbade the planned book-burning that was scheduled to take place in front of the University building.
stops.quote_source: Heidegger, Der Spiegel interview (1966), trans. Richardson
suggested_refs: Karl Jaspers's 1945 assessment for the Freiburg denazification committee

stops.name: Badenweiler, the clinic at Schloss Hausbaden
stops.date_confidence: attested to the winter of 1945-1946; no precise dates of admission or discharge are documented, and the entry date here is a convention. The institution is named in the sources as the private psychiatric clinic Schloss Hausbaden near Badenweiler, where Viktor von Gebsattel was chief physician after the war.
stops.campa: Over the winter he breaks down. He is treated at Schloss Hausbaden near Badenweiler, the psychiatric clinic where Viktor von Gebsattel is chief physician. He is fifty-six years old, dismissed, banned, publicly disgraced, and still the most influential philosopher in Europe. Biographers call it depression, a nervous collapse, a psychosomatic crisis; no retrospective diagnosis is documented and none would be worth much. Neither the date of admission nor the date of discharge is written down anywhere reachable.
suggested_refs: The private clinic Schloss Hausbaden near Badenweiler under Viktor Emil von Gebsattel

stops.name: Freiburg-Zähringen, the Letter on Humanism
stops.date_confidence: attested: Beaufret's questions are dated 10 November 1946, the letter was written in December 1946, and it was reworked for publication in 1947. The coordinate is the house at Rötebuckweg 47 in Freiburg-Zähringen, his working address; the exact place of writing is not separately confirmed.
stops.campa: Jean Beaufret writes from Paris in November with a question: how can meaning be given back to the word humanism? Heidegger answers at length in December and reworks the answer for publication the following year. The letter declines Jean-Paul Sartre's existentialism as one more humanism, one more metaphysics of the subject, with man still standing in the middle of it. The text makes him readable in France at the moment he is unemployable in Germany, and Beaufret becomes the door. Language, he writes, is the house of Being.
suggested_refs: Brief über den Humanismus (written December 1946, published 1947); Sartre's L'existentialisme est un humanisme (1946)

stops.name: Freiburg, classified Mitläufer
stops.date_confidence: attested to March 1949; the day is not given.
stops.campa: The Freiburg denazification commission classifies him Mitläufer, fellow traveller, the lowest of the incrimination categories, carrying no penalty beyond what has already fallen on him. Four years of hearings end in a word that means he went along. The classification satisfies nobody. It is far too light for anyone who has read the rectoral address, and far too heavy for a man who has spent four years explaining that he was protecting the university. The teaching ban stands another year and a half after the verdict.
suggested_refs: The Freiburg denazification file and the Mitläufer classification of March 1949

stops.name: Bremen, the lectures at the Club zu Bremen
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1949; the month is conventional. The venue is identified as the Club zu Bremen from the general literature on the lecture series and was not re-verified against a primary programme.
stops.campa: Invited by the Club zu Bremen, barred from lecturing at any university, he delivers the lectures in which mechanised agriculture, the manufacture of atomic weapons and the production of corpses in gas chambers and extermination camps are placed inside one and the same technological essence. It is among the very few occasions on which he speaks of the camps at all. He does not pause to mark any difference between the terms of that list. Readers have taken the sentence as recognition, as levelling and as evasion, and the text gives no way to decide which.
stops.quote: Everything is functioning. That is precisely what is awesome, that everything functions, that the functioning propels everything more and more toward further functioning, and that technicity increasingly dislodges man and uproots him from the earth.
stops.quote_source: Heidegger, Der Spiegel interview (1966), trans. Richardson, on the same technological essence the Bremen lectures had named seventeen years earlier
suggested_refs: The Bremen lectures of 1949, Gesamtausgabe 79

stops.name: Freiburg, the ban lifted and emeritus status
stops.date_confidence: the sources give 1950 and 1951 for the readmission to teaching and the grant of emeritus status; the discrepancy is not resolved here and the month and day default.
stops.campa: The ban is lifted, Freiburg readmits him to teaching, and he lectures as emeritus. The work of these years has left the analytic of Dasein behind. He writes about Gestell, the enframing that turns everything into standing reserve; about dwelling and building; about Gelassenheit, releasement, a thinking that does not grasp; about Ereignis. What he is asking is no longer what it means to be, but what it would take to be addressed. The prose turns toward the poets.
stops.quote: Questioning is the piety of thought.
stops.quote_source: Heidegger, closing line of 'Die Frage nach der Technik,' quoted by himself within the Der Spiegel interview (1966), trans. Richardson
suggested_refs: 'Die Frage nach der Technik' and 'Bauen Wohnen Denken,' from the lectures of the 1950s

segments.name: Zollikon, Provence, and the Voice Kept in a Drawer

stops.name: Zollikon, the seminars for the doctors
stops.date_confidence: attested to the span 1959-1969; the month and day of the first seminar are not given here.
stops.campa: At the house of the psychiatrist Medard Boss in Zollikon, above Zürich, he begins a decade of seminars for physicians: how to question a patient phenomenologically, what a body is when it is not an object, what illness is when the ill person is the one who has a world. He criticises Ludwig Binswanger's use of Sein und Zeit as a psychology of the subject, which is precisely the reading the book was written against. The doctors take notes. Boss edits the protocols into a volume afterwards, and the seminars run to 1969.
suggested_refs: Zollikoner Seminare, ed. Medard Boss, from the protocols of 1959-1969

stops.name: Athens, the Acropolis at last
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The travel years 1962 and 1967 are attested; the Acropolis stands here as the emblematic site rather than a confirmed itinerary point, and no month, day or route survives in the sources consulted.
stops.campa: He goes to Greece at seventy-two, after forty years of writing about the Greek beginning and more than one journey cancelled before departure. He walks up to the Acropolis. The record of the visit is thin: two travel years, 1962 and 1967, some notes, no itinerary that survives in anything reachable. Whether the stones answered to what forty years of reading Heraclitus and Parmenides had built in him, or whether arriving was a small disappointment the notes decline to name, the record does not say.
suggested_refs: Aufenthalte (1962 Greek travel journal), Gesamtausgabe 75

stops.name: Le Thor, the seminars in René Char's Provence
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1966, 1968 and 1969; the month is conventional and the coordinate marks the village of Le Thor, not a specific house.
stops.campa: The poet René Char keeps him in Provence for private seminars, held in 1966, 1968 and 1969, with French philosophers and poets in the room and the Vaucluse heat outside it. There is no university here, no rectorate, no denazification file. The man who once told the German university what its self-assertion consisted in spends his last teaching years as a guest of the country that had been on the other side. There are cypresses, a handful of listeners, and a German in his late seventies talking under a tree.
suggested_refs: Vier Seminare (Le Thor 1966, 1968, 1969 and Zähringen 1973), Gesamtausgabe 15

stops.name: Freiburg, the interview sealed until his death
stops.date_confidence: attested to 23 September 1966, at his Freiburg home. One source additionally names Todtnauberg as a possible venue; the verification pass rejects it.
stops.campa: Rudolf Augstein and Georg Wolff come to the house at Zähringen with a tape recorder. He talks for hours: the rectorate, the Party, the book-burning he says he forbade, the technicity that has outrun every politics, and finally what can be done about it, which is nothing philosophy can do. His condition is that not a word appear while he is alive. He corrects the transcript and signs it. The file goes into a drawer at Der Spiegel and stays there ten years.
stops.quote: Only a god can save us. The only possibility available to us is that by thinking and poetizing we prepare a readiness for the appearance of a god, or for the absence of a god in our decline, insofar as in view of the absent god we are in a state of decline.
stops.quote_source: Heidegger, Der Spiegel interview 'Nur noch ein Gott kann uns retten,' recorded 23 September 1966, published 31 May 1976, trans. William J. Richardson
suggested_refs: 'Nur noch ein Gott kann uns retten,' Der Spiegel 30/23 (31 May 1976)
sources: Der Spiegel interview (1966), trans. Richardson, ditext.com/heidegger/interview.html

stops.name: Todtnauberg, Paul Celan at the hut
stops.date_confidence: the visit is attested to 25 July 1967; the hut coordinate is approximate, as at the 1922 stop.
stops.campa: Paul Celan, whose mother and father were murdered by Germans, climbs to the hut on the twenty-fifth of July and writes his name in the guest book. The two men walk out into the high moor. Celan writes 'Todtnauberg' afterwards, with its hope, in the heart, for a thinker's word to come. There is no transcript of anything either of them said. Nobody knows whether the word came, whether it was refused, or whether the talk stayed on arnica and eyebright and the well outside the door.
suggested_refs: Paul Celan, 'Todtnauberg' (1967); the Todtnauberg guest book entry of 25 July 1967

segments.name: The Edition of Last Hand and the Ground at Meßkirch

stops.name: Freiburg-Zähringen, the edition of last hand
stops.date_confidence: the Gesamtausgabe is attested as beginning publication with Klostermann in 1975, in his lifetime; the month and day default, and one claim that the edition stood complete at 106 volumes in 2025 is rejected here as unsupported.
stops.campa: With Vittorio Klostermann he fixes the shape of the collected works, and the first volume appears while he is still alive: an Ausgabe letzter Hand, an edition of the last hand, ordered not by chronology but by kind, lecture courses beside books beside unpublished treatises, the private notebooks placed at the end. No critical apparatus. No variant readings. Ways, not works, is the motto he sets at its head. Fifty years on the edition has passed a hundred volumes and is not finished.
suggested_refs: The Heidegger Gesamtausgabe, Vittorio Klostermann, Frankfurt am Main, from 1975

stops.name: Freiburg-Zähringen, death in the house
stops.date_confidence: attested to 26 May 1976; no detailed terminal diagnosis is recorded in the reachable sources.
stops.campa: He dies at home in Freiburg-Zähringen on the twenty-sixth of May, eighty-six years old. No terminal diagnosis is set down in anything reachable; the general accounts say old age. He had gone on working to the end, on the ordering of the collected edition and on the notebooks nobody outside the house had read. Five days later Der Spiegel prints the interview he gave ten years before, and West Germany reads in a dead man's voice that only a god can save us now. The body goes to Meßkirch.
suggested_refs: The house at Rötebuckweg 47, Freiburg-Zähringen

stops.name: Meßkirch, the grave with a single star
stops.date_confidence: the burial on 28 May 1976 beside his parents and Bernhard Welte's graveside address are attested. That the rite was a Catholic burial rite conducted by Welte, and that Heidegger had requested it in advance, is not confirmed by anything reachable. The cemetery coordinate is approximate: the sources carry three different values for this one grave.
stops.campa: On the twenty-eighth of May he is buried in the Meßkirch cemetery beside Friedrich and Johanna Heidegger. Bernhard Welte, theologian and fellow son of the town, gives the graveside address. That the rite was Catholic is reported; that Heidegger asked for it beforehand is not confirmed by any source reachable here. On the stone there is a star. It is set there for his own sentence: that to think is to confine yourself to a single thought that one day stands still like a star in the world's sky.
suggested_refs: The Heidegger family grave in the Meßkirch municipal cemetery; the Martin-Heidegger-Museum in the east wing of Schloss Meßkirch and its archive of photographs and recordings
